prompt: A scan counts each new running maximum in a uniformly random permutation of distinct finite values. Why do record updates become less frequent later?

options.text: Later positions are guaranteed to contain smaller values.
options.explanation: Uniform random order gives no such deterministic guarantee.

options.text: Every possible number of updates is equally likely.
options.explanation: Counts arise from different numbers of permutations.

options.text: A later value must beat more earlier values.
options.explanation: Among a longer prefix, only one equally likely position contains its largest value.

options.text: The scan stops comparing after the first record.
options.explanation: It must still examine every item.

workedExample: The first value sets a record automatically. At a later position, ask whether it is the largest in the prefix seen so far. More competing positions lower that probability; expected updates grow slowly even though the scan examines every element.

link.title: Introduction to Probability — Grinstead and Snell

prompt: A cache warmer has at least two shards and independently chooses a uniformly random shard on each request, with replacement. Why does completing coverage take longer than making one request per shard on average?

options.text: The last missing shard becomes increasingly likely on each miss.
options.explanation: Its selection probability remains fixed under this model.

options.text: Late requests mostly revisit shards already seen.
options.explanation: The chance of discovering a new shard falls as the missing set shrinks.

options.text: A shard becomes impossible to visit after other shards are visited.
options.explanation: Every shard retains positive selection probability.

options.text: Each request is guaranteed to visit a new shard.

workedExample: Break coverage into stages based on how many shards remain unseen. Early stages have many ways to make progress; the last stage has only one. Its long geometric wait explains the extra work.
